part_title: Generative AI and Foundation Models — What They Are and How to Choose
review_basis: Original Module 04 numbered WebP slides 1–3 individually inspected: actual labels, diagrams and example probabilities narrated in visual sequence.

scenes.title: Generative AI: from patterns to new content
scenes.narration: Begin on the left with the input prompt: a serene mountain lake at sunrise with a wooden dock and reflections. A prompt is simply the instruction we give to an AI model. Follow the blue arrow to the trained foundation model in the middle. During training, a model learns statistical patterns in examples, such as relationships among words, images, and descriptions. During inference, when we send a new request, it uses those learned patterns to produce a response. Follow the second arrow to the generated image and text on the right. The result is new content rather than a predetermined class label. Notice the warning: generated images or explanations may be incomplete, inaccurate or biased and require review. At the bottom the slide contrasts generation with classification. Generation produces something new, such as an image or paragraph. Classification chooses among predefined categories, such as spam and not spam. Question: if we want to identify whether an email is spam, must we use generative AI? No. A classifier may be simpler and more appropriate.

scenes.title: Foundation models can serve many tasks
scenes.narration: Follow the foundation model diagram from left to right. The left panel shows broad unlabeled text and image data: articles, documents, books and pictures. Pretraining means learning general patterns from this broad collection before a particular user's task is known. The central network represents a foundation model, or family of models, that can be prompted or adapted for useful tasks. On the upper right, a text-capable model can summarize an article or answer a question about a passage. The example prompt asks for the main idea of a passage; the output is a concise answer. The lower right illustrates an image-capable model generating a headset concept picture from a description. A key caution appears beside both groups: not every model supports every kind of input or output. Modality means the form of information, such as text or images. Some models support only text, some only images, and some multiple modalities. The takeaway says to select a model that actually supports the required task and modality. Decision check: can we assume a model that summarizes text will also create pictures? No; verify the particular model's supported capabilities.

scenes.title: Foundation models: reuse, providers and licensing
scenes.narration: This dense slide combines several practical choices, so follow its sections carefully. Top left, a foundation model learns general patterns from broad data and can support summaries, questions, code and other tasks. The top middle reminds us that large-scale pretraining can consume enormous datasets, computing resources and expert engineering. The cost boxes are examples, not a fixed universal price. Top right, the flow starts with broad data, passes through pretraining, and reaches a reusable foundation model. Organizations can adapt it with prompts, retrieval augmented generation, called R A G, or supported fine tuning. These techniques are different from training an entire foundation model from scratch. In the lower left, distinguish the model itself from an application: a chat interface can connect a model with workflows, tools and user features. The center gives provider examples including Amazon, Meta, Google, Anthropic and OpenAI. Availability depends on model, service and Region. On the lower right, licensing distinguishes downloadable open weights, open source under specific licenses, and proprietary commercial access. Downloadable weights do not automatically grant unrestricted commercial use. Finally, compare managed API access at the bottom left with self-hosting model weights at the bottom right. Managed access reduces infrastructure operations; self-hosting gives more control but increases security, scaling, maintenance and cost responsibilities. Check: is choosing an open-weight model the same as having no license or hosting obligations? Absolutely not.
